newsitem.title: INDIA: India to ease business travel from Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: India to ease business travel from Pakistan.

text.p: India said it favoured strengthening economic ties with Pakistan and would soon take steps to promote business travel between the two longtime enemies.

Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral on Friday told a delegation from the Pakistan Overseas Investment Chamber of Commerce that "steps will be announced to facilitate the issuance of business visas", a ministry spokesman told reporters in the Indian capital. He did not elaborate.

"The Indian minister conveyed that it was in the interest of the government to deepen commercial and economic contacts between the two countries and he emphasised that this interaction would be for mutual benefit," the spokesman said.
The Pakistani delegation told Gujral there were good prospects for forging commercial and economic links, and that the two countries' economies complemented each other, the spokesman said.

It is difficult for Indian and Pakistani nationals to obtain visas for cross-border travel because of longstanding tensions. Exceptions are sometimes made for those with relatives across the border and for some government officials and businessmen.

Gujral, who assumed his post when the government administration of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda took power last June, has pressed for greater contact between citizens of the two countries as a means of alleviating political tension.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over the disputed province of Kashmir.
Pakistani prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif's victory in recent general elections has raised hopes that the two countries could soon resume high-level peace talks which broke off in early 1994.
Deve Gowda said on Thursday he favoured a resumption of talks but that New Delhi would never surrender the two-thirds of Kashmir which it controls. Pakistan controls the other third.
Pakistan said on Friday that Deve Gowda's offer for talks was useless unless the subject of Kashmir was on the table.
